models.title: Grinold-Kroner decomposition of expected equity return
models.summary: Expected equity return as dividend yield plus EPS growth (total earnings growth minus shares-outstanding growth) plus P/E repricing change.

relationship.locator: PDF: LM2 Forecasting Asset Class Returns, printed p. 84 (PDF p. 94), Eq. 1
relationship.translation_notes: Source expresses rates as percentages; record uses decimal form (unit 1), so 2% is 0.02 with no conversion factor in the expression. dy is dividend yield D/P; gE total earnings growth %ΔE; gS shares-outstanding growth %ΔS (negative under net buybacks); gPE P/E repricing %ΔP/E. The ≈ reflects approximation, not a fitted residual. Dimensional check: all terms dimensionless rates, sum is a dimensionless rate.

variables.definition: Dividend yield: current dividends per share divided by price, in decimal form
variables.context: same equity market and forecast horizon as ERe

variables.definition: Expected percentage change in total earnings over the horizon, in decimal form
variables.context: same equity market and forecast horizon as ERe

variables.definition: Expected percentage change in shares outstanding; negative under net share repurchases, in decimal form
variables.context: same equity market and forecast horizon as ERe
variables.domain: Finite decimal growth rate; greater than -1 (shares cannot fall more than 100%)

variables.definition: Expected percentage change in the price-to-earnings ratio (repricing return), in decimal form
variables.context: same equity market and forecast horizon as ERe
variables.domain: Finite decimal growth rate; greater than -1

variables.definition: Expected equity market return over the horizon, in decimal form
variables.context: same equity market and forecast horizon as inputs

assumptions: The decomposition applies to a broad equity market over the stated forecast horizon with consistent timing of yield, growth, and repricing terms.
Source assumption: repurchases are captured through the change in shares outstanding, so (gE − gS) is EPS growth.
limitations: Approximate identity (source uses ≈); compounding interactions between components over long horizons are not modeled.
Excludes taxes, fees, and implementation shortfall; not investment advice.

references.method: Direct substitution: 0.02 + (0.04 − (−0.01)) + 0.005 = 0.075. Independently constructed arithmetic check.

models.inverse_notes: Linear in each input: dy = ERe − (gE − gS) − gPE; gE = ERe − dy + gS − gPE; gS = gE − (ERe − dy − gPE); gPE = ERe − dy − (gE − gS). No singularities (no division). Substitution check: ERe=0.075 with dy=0.02, gE=0.04, gS=−0.01 recovers gPE=0.005. Algebraic inversion only; causal interpretation of repricing is not established by inversion.

models.title: Long-run commercial real estate expected return from cap rate and NOI growth
models.summary: Steady-state expected return on commercial real estate equals the capitalization rate plus the constant NOI growth rate (Gordon growth applied to property).

relationship.original_equation: E(Rre) = Cap rate + NOI growth rate
relationship.locator: PDF: LM2 Forecasting Real Estate Returns, printed p. 94 (PDF p. 104), Eq. 7
relationship.translation_notes: Source expresses rates as percentages; record uses decimal form (unit 1) with no conversion factor inlined. Cap rate is current-period NOI divided by property value. Long-run steady-state NOI growth is reasonably close to GDP growth per the source. Dimensional check: dimensionless + dimensionless = dimensionless rate.

variables.definition: Capitalization rate: current-period net operating income divided by property value, in decimal form
variables.context: same commercial property market and steady-state horizon as ERre

variables.definition: Constant long-run steady-state growth rate of net operating income, in decimal form
variables.context: same commercial property market and steady-state horizon as ERre
variables.domain: Finite decimal growth rate; below the discount rate for Gordon-model validity

variables.definition: Long-run expected (required) rate of return on commercial real estate, in decimal form
variables.context: same commercial property market and steady-state horizon as inputs

assumptions: Source assumption: NOI grows at a constant rate in perpetuity (Gordon growth applied to property).
Steady-state horizon; anticipated cap-rate change is zero over the long run.
limitations: Long-run steady state only; finite-horizon repricing from cap-rate change requires the companion cap-rate-change record.
A portion of operating income may be reinvested, so the cap rate is not strictly a cash flow yield (per source note).

models.title: Finite-horizon real estate expected return with cap-rate change
models.summary: Over finite horizons, expected real estate return equals cap rate plus NOI growth minus the percentage change in the cap rate (repricing term).

relationship.original_equation: E(Rre) = Cap rate + NOI growth rate − %ΔCap rate
relationship.locator: PDF: LM2 Forecasting Real Estate Returns, printed p. 94 (PDF p. 104), Eq. 8
relationship.translation_notes: Source expresses rates as percentages; record uses decimal form (unit 1). dcap is the relative (percentage) change in the cap rate over the horizon, e.g. (5.5−5.7)/5.7 ≈ −0.035. A falling cap rate (negative dcap) raises expected return via price appreciation. Analogous to Grinold-Kroner repricing but with no share-buyback term, per source. Dimensional check: all dimensionless rates.

variables.definition: Expected rate of return on commercial real estate over the finite horizon, in decimal form

assumptions: Finite horizon over which the cap rate moves from its starting level to the anticipated ending level.

models.title: Mean-variance utility (certainty equivalent) in decimal form
models.summary: Investor utility for an asset mix as expected return minus one-half the risk aversion coefficient times variance, with all rates in decimals.

relationship.original_equation: Um = E(Rm) − 0.005 λ σm² (percent form); = E(Rm) − 0.5 λ σm² in decimals
relationship.locator: PDF: LM4 Mean–Variance Optimization Overview, printed p. 200 (PDF p. 210), Eq. 1
relationship.translation_notes: Source Eq. 1 uses 0.005 because E(Rm) and σm are entered as percentages with % signs omitted (e.g. 10.0, 20). Record uses decimal form (unit 1), so the scale factor is 0.5 per the source's own decimal restatement: 0.10 − 0.5(2)(0.04) = 0.06. The 0.5 is a pure arithmetic scaling literal explained here, not an inlined unit conversion. Dimensional check: dimensionless − (dimensionless × dimensionless²) = dimensionless.

variables.definition: Expected return of asset mix m over the single-period horizon, in decimal form
variables.context: same asset mix m and single-period horizon as Um

variables.definition: Investor risk aversion coefficient: rate at which the investor forgoes expected return for less variance
variables.context: same investor and asset mix m as Um
variables.domain: Nonnegative finite coefficient; zero is the risk-neutral boundary

variables.definition: Expected standard deviation of return for asset mix m, in decimal form
variables.context: same asset mix m and single-period horizon as Um
variables.domain: Nonnegative finite volatility; zero is the risk-free boundary

variables.definition: Investor utility (certainty-equivalent return) of asset mix m, in decimal form
variables.context: same asset mix m, investor, and horizon as inputs

assumptions: Single-period mean–variance framework: utility depends only on expected return and variance of the asset mix.
Source assumption: decimal inputs use the 0.5 scaling; percent inputs would use 0.005 with % signs omitted.
limitations: Captures only mean–variance preferences; skewness, kurtosis, and non-variance risk notions (e.g. shortfall probability) are excluded — the source pairs this with a separate safety-first ratio.
The risk aversion coefficient must be estimated separately; the equation does not determine it.

sources.title: The Risk Aversion Coefficient (Desjardins Online Brokerage, citing Bodie–Kane–Marcus)
sources.version: Educational article citing Investments by Bodie, Kane, Marcus, Perrakis & Ryan (2014), McGraw Hill Ryerson, 8th Canadian ed., p. 156
sources.locator: Utility formula section: U = E(r) − 0.5 × A × σ² with two worked examples
sources.evidence: Page presents the mean-variance utility formula U = E(r) − 0.5·A·σ² with worked decimal examples (0.06 − 0.5·2·0.16² = 3.44%), confirming the decimal-form scaling used in this record.
sources.redistribution: Short original paraphrase and single-formula transcription only; no extended quotation

references.method: Source's decimal restatement: 0.10 − 0.5(2)(0.04) = 0.06. Direct substitution matches.
references.provenance: Published result: LM4 text, printed p. 200 (PDF p. 210)

references.method: Example 1 allocation C (5.25% return, 5% volatility, λ=2) converted to decimals: 0.0525 − 0.5·2·0.0025 = 0.05, matching the published UC = 5.0%.
references.provenance: Published result: LM4 Example 1, printed p. 207 (PDF p. 217), with documented percent-to-decimal conversion

rejection_cases.reason: Negative risk aversion contradicts the stated risk-averse penalty framing (guard lam >= 0); risk-seeking preferences need a different model.
Volatility is a required input; expected return and risk aversion alone cannot determine utility.

models.inverse_notes: ERm = Um + 0.5·lam·sig² always; lam = 2·(ERm − Um)/sig² requires sig ≠ 0 (if sig = 0 then Um = ERm and lam is undetermined); sig = sqrt(2·(ERm − Um)/lam) requires lam > 0 and ERm ≥ Um. Substitution check: Um=0.06, lam=2, sig=0.2 recovers ERm=0.10. Algebraic only; risk aversion is estimated, not caused, by inversion.
